data.raw_text:
Usually when I tell a WW2 story it's second-hand. As in, I got it from the guy who experienced it. This story is third-hand. It's from the son of the man who experienced it. It was a long account, and I heard it in the 80s, but I remember these two facts: 

His unit had to attack Iloilo City in the Philippines (Panay). They were practically panicked, despite the fact that they had already seen action in New Britain. His dad explained - "We knew jungle fighting. We had never fought house-to-house. We knew that we'd have to learn urban fighting as we went along, which meant we'd suffer extra casualties." That made sense. 

Second, his dad was a medic, and I learned that when a medic dosed a casualty with some drug, he'd use chalk to write what he'd done on the guy's helmet. For instance, if he gave him a unit of morphine, he'd chalk "1M".  So when the guy got to the aid station, the doctors would know what he had. This made a ton of sense to me. 

In an earlier Pacific War post I talked about how the ubiquitous Japanese Type 89 mortar was highly effective. A lot comments missed the point, saying stuff like, "The US (or the UK) mortars were better." Yeah I'm sure they were in some ways. The advantage of the Type 89 was first that it weighed just 10 lbs. The US 60mm mortar weighed more than 40 lbs. The UK 2 inch mortar was similar to the Type 89. 

But the other huge advantage of the Type 89 had nothing to do with its quality. It was that they were so common. Every Japanese platoon had 3 Type 89s. A company had 12. By comparison, British and American companies only had 3 mortars for a company (the British split it up 1 per platoon, while the Americans kept them together). 

So the sheer amount of mortar fire you'd encounter facing the Japanese was 4 times more, even if each individual shell was slightly less accurate. It probably made up for their complete lack of submachine guns. 

Anyway I thought it was interesting.
